jp: 部長[ぶちょう]、私[わたし]が今[いま]すぐ資料[しりょう]を取[と]りに{参[まい]ります|kg-ken-special}。
en: Department head, I will go and fetch the documents right now.
why: I go somewhere, speaking to a superior, so the humble 参る is used; いらっしゃる would honour me.

jp: 来週[らいしゅう]から出張[しゅっちょう]で大阪[おおさか]へ{参[まい]ります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I will be going to Osaka on a business trip from next week (said politely to a client).
why: The speaker's own trip is expressed with the humble-polite 参る, never with the honorific いらっしゃる.

jp: 空[そら]が暗[くら]くなって{参[まい]りました|kg-ken-special}。
en: The sky has been getting dark.
why: 〜て参ります expresses a change that gradually comes on; 参る is the polite form of 〜てくる.

jp: 先生[せんせい]、母[はは]が来週[らいしゅう]学校[がっこう]に{参[まい]ります/伺[うかが]います|kg-ken-special}ので、よろしくお願[ねが]いします。
en: Teacher, my mother will come to the school next week, so please look after her.
why: My own mother's coming is described humbly to the teacher; いらっしゃる would honour my family member.

jp: 毎朝[まいあさ]、歩[ある]いて会社[かいしゃ]に{参[まい]ります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I go to the office on foot every morning (said politely to a superior).
why: Going to the office is my own movement, so the humble 参る is needed; おる means 'be', not 'go'.

jp: バスはまもなく{参[まい]ります|kg-ken-special}ので、少[すこ]しお待[ま]ちください。
en: The bus will arrive shortly, so please wait a moment.
why: In announcements the polite 参る is used for coming vehicles; 申す means 'say' and おる means 'be'.

jp: 昨日[きのう]は友達[ともだち]と映画[えいが]を見[み]に{参[まい]りました|kg-ken-special}。
en: Yesterday I went to see a movie with a friend (said politely to a teacher).
why: My own going is expressed with 参る when speaking up to a superior; いらっしゃる honours others only.

jp: 先生[せんせい]、お荷物[にもつ]をお持[も]ちして{参[まい]りました|kg-ken-special}。
en: Teacher, I have brought your luggage.
why: お持ちして参る means 'I brought it here'; the speaker's own coming uses the humble 参る.

jp: 初[はじ]めまして、山田[やまだ]と{申[もう]します|kg-ken-special}。
en: How do you do, my name is Yamada.
why: Giving my own name uses the humble 申す; おっしゃる is only for what others say.

jp: 田中[たなか]と{申[もう]します|kg-ken-special}。青山[あおやま]商事[しょうじ]の者[もの]です。
en: My name is Tanaka. I am from Aoyama Trading.
why: In self-introductions, 〜と申します is the humble way to say what one is called.

jp: 担任[たんにん]の先生[せんせい]には、明日[あした]は休[やす]むと{申[もう]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I told my homeroom teacher that I would be absent tomorrow.
why: I am the one who said it, so the humble 申す fits; おっしゃる would honour me.

jp: 母[はは]が「いつもありがとうございます」と{申[もう]しておりました|kg-ken-special}。
en: My mother said, 'Thank you for always (helping us)' (reported to someone outside the family).
d: おっしゃっていました
召[め]し上[あ]がっていました
参[まい]っておりました
why: My own mother is on my side, so her saying is reported with 申す, not the honorific おっしゃる.

jp: 正直[しょうじき]に{申[もう]しますと|kg-ken-special}、この計画[けいかく]はかなり難[むずか]しいです。
en: To be honest with you, this plan is quite difficult.
why: 〜と申しますと introduces what I am about to say; the verb 'say' is the humble 申す.

jp: この件[けん]の担当[たんとう]は、鈴木[すずき]と{申[もう]します|kg-ken-special}。
en: The person in charge of this matter is called Suzuki (said to a client).
why: A colleague on my side is named with 〜と申します, as Suzuki is not to be honoured before a client.

jp: 父[ちち]は毎日[まいにち]「早[はや]く寝[ね]なさい」と{申[もう]します|kg-ken-special}。
en: My father says 'Go to bed early' every day (said to a teacher).
why: My father is part of my side when talking to a teacher, so his words are reported with 申す.

jp: 先日[せんじつ]お電話[でんわ]で{申[もう]しました/申[もう]し上[あ]げました|kg-ken-special}とおり、来月[らいげつ]から値上[ねあ]げいたします。
en: As I said on the phone the other day, prices will go up from next month.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: What the speaker said earlier to the customer is expressed with the humble 申す.

jp: 部長[ぶちょう]のお宅[たく]で、おいしいカレーを{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: At the department head's home I ate some delicious curry.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
拝見[はいけん]しました
why: I ate at a superior's house, so the humble いただく is used; 召し上がる would honour me.

jp: では、遠慮[えんりょ]なく{いただきます|kg-ken-special}。
en: Well then, I will gladly have some (said to the host before eating).
why: The speaker's own eating, said politely to the host, is いただきます; 召し上がる is for the host's eating.

jp: 取引先[とりひきさき]の方[かた]に、おいしいケーキを{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I received some delicious cake from someone at a client company.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: I receive something from a person I respect, so the humble いただく is used; に marks the giver here.

jp: 私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]からお手紙[てがみ]を{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I received a letter from my teacher.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: With 私は as the receiver, the humble いただく is right; くださる would need the teacher as subject.

jp: 今朝[けさ]はパンとコーヒーを{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: This morning I had bread and coffee (said to a superior).
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: いただく is also the humble verb for eating or drinking, used when I speak to someone I respect.

jp: 母[はは]は先生[せんせい]から卒業[そつぎょう]のお祝[いわ]いを{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: My mother received a graduation gift from the teacher.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: My mother is the receiver and the teacher the giver, so the humble いただく fits.

jp: では、お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて、もう一杯[いっぱい]{いただきます|kg-ken-special}。
en: Then, taking you at your word, I will have another cup.
why: Accepting another serving from a host is humble いただきます; 召し上がる would describe the host's eating.

jp: 私[わたし]たちは課長[かちょう]から会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]を{いただきました|kg-ken-special}。
en: We received the meeting documents from the section chief.
why: We are the receivers and the section chief is the giver, so humble いただく is used.

jp: 先生[せんせい]の作品[さくひん]を{拝見[はいけん]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I looked at my teacher's work.
d: ご覧[らん]になりました
拝借[はいしゃく]しました
お目[め]にかかりました
why: I look at something belonging to a respected person, so the humble 拝見する is used.

jp: お客様[きゃくさま]、パスポートを{拝見[はいけん]します|kg-ken-special}。
en: Sir, I will have a look at your passport (hotel clerk to a guest).
d: 拝借[はいしゃく]します
拝聴[はいちょう]します
why: The clerk looks at the guest's passport; 拝見する humbly means 'to see'.

jp: お送[おく]りいただいた見積書[みつもりしょ]を{拝見[はいけん]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I have looked over the estimate you sent me.
d: ご覧[らん]になりました
拝聴[はいちょう]しました
why: I examine a document from a respected business partner, so the humble 拝見する fits.

jp: お客様[きゃくさま]、チケットを{拝見[はいけん]します|kg-ken-special}。
en: Madam, I will check your ticket.
d: 拝借[はいしゃく]します
why: The staff member looks at the guest's ticket; the humble 拝見する is the standard word.

jp: 先生[せんせい]のお宅[たく]で、珍[めずら]しい絵[え]を{拝見[はいけん]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: At my teacher's home I saw a rare painting.
d: ご覧[らん]になりました
お目[め]にかかりました
拝借[はいしゃく]しました
why: I saw something at a superior's house; 拝見する is humble, while ご覧になる would honour me.

jp: 部長[ぶちょう]がお書[か]きになった企画書[きかくしょ]を、昨日[きのう]{拝見[はいけん]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: Yesterday I looked at the proposal that the department head wrote.
d: ご覧[らん]になりました
拝借[はいしゃく]しました
お目[め]にかかりました
why: The department head wrote it (honorific), and I looked at it, so the humble 拝見する is needed.

jp: 展覧会[てんらんかい]で、先生[せんせい]の絵[え]を初[はじ]めて{拝見[はいけん]しました|kg-ken-special}。
en: At the exhibition I saw my teacher's paintings for the first time.
d: ご覧[らん]になりました
拝借[はいしゃく]しました
お目[め]にかかりました
why: I viewed the respected teacher's paintings, and the humble verb for seeing is 拝見する.

jp: 母[はは]は先生[せんせい]の写真[しゃしん]を{拝見[はいけん]して|kg-ken-special}、とても喜[よろこ]んでいました。
en: My mother looked at the teacher's photographs and was very pleased.
why: My mother is on my side, and she looked at a respected person's photos, so humble 拝見する is used.

jp: 資料[しりょう]は私[わたし]が準備[じゅんび]{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: I will prepare the materials myself.
why: I offer to do something, so the humble いたす replaces する; なさる would honour me.

jp: お客様[きゃくさま]、お席[せき]までご案内[あんない]{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: Madam, I will show you to your seat.
why: The staff member does the guiding for the guest, so the humble いたす is used.

jp: 本日[ほんじつ]は私[わたし]が司会[しかい]を{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: Today I will be the master of ceremonies.
why: The speaker introduces what they will do, so the humble いたす stands for する.

jp: 明日[あした]、お品物[しなもの]をお届[とど]け{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: I will deliver your goods tomorrow.
why: お〜いたす is a humble pattern for my own action for the customer's benefit.

jp: 大変[たいへん]失礼[しつれい]{いたしました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I am very sorry (for my rudeness).
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: An apology for my own conduct uses the humble いたす; なさる cannot be used for oneself.

jp: ただ今[いま]、確認[かくにん]{いたします|kg-ken-special}ので、少々[しょうしょう]お待[ま]ちください。
en: I will check right now, so please wait a moment.
why: The clerk checks for the customer, so the humble いたす is used for 'do'.

jp: 来月[らいげつ]から、担当[たんとう]を変更[へんこう]{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: From next month we will change the person in charge.
why: A company announcing its own action to customers uses the humble いたす.

jp: 弟[おとうと]がご迷惑[めいわく]をおかけしました。私[わたし]が代[か]わりにお詫[わ]び{いたします|kg-ken-special}。
en: My brother caused you trouble. I will apologise in his place.
why: I apologise on my side's behalf, so the humble いたす is right and the honorific なさる is not.

jp: 申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません、鈴木[すずき]はただ今[いま]席[せき]を外[はず]して{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I am sorry, Mr. Suzuki is away from his desk at the moment (said to a caller).
why: To outsiders my colleague is on my side, so his state is described with おる, not いらっしゃる.

jp: 三年前[さんねんまえ]から京都[きょうと]に住[す]んで{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I have been living in Kyoto for three years (said politely to a superior).
why: I describe my own state, so ておる replaces ている; ていらっしゃる would honour me.

jp: 毎日[まいにち]、駅[えき]の前[まえ]の店[みせ]で働[はたら]いて{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I work at a shop in front of the station every day (said politely to a superior).
why: The speaker's own ongoing action is expressed with the humble 〜ておる.

jp: ご連絡[れんらく]をお待[ま]ちして{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: I look forward to hearing from you.
why: The speaker waits for the other person's contact, which is expressed with お待ちしております.

jp: 母[はは]は今[いま]台所[だいどころ]で料理[りょうり]をして{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: My mother is cooking in the kitchen now (said to a visitor).
why: My own mother is on my side when speaking to a guest, so ておる is used rather than ていらっしゃる.

jp: 兄[あに]は今[いま]、海外[かいがい]に留学[りゅうがく]して{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: My older brother is studying abroad now (said to a teacher).
why: A family member is described humbly to an outsider, so 〜ておる is used for the ongoing state.

jp: 今日[きょう]は一日中[いちにちじゅう]会社[かいしゃ]に{おります|kg-ken-special}ので、いつでもお電話[でんわ]ください。
en: I will be at the office all day, so please call me any time.
why: My own presence somewhere is expressed with the humble おる; ございます is only for things.

jp: 父[ちち]は病院[びょういん]で医者[いしゃ]をして{おります|kg-ken-special}。
en: My father works as a doctor at a hospital (said to a teacher).
why: My father's work is described humbly to an outsider, so 〜ておる is used.

jp: 先生[せんせい]、ちょっと{伺[うかが]いたいのですが|kg-ken-special}。
en: Teacher, there is something I would like to ask you.
d: おっしゃりたいのですが
申[もう]したいのですが
召[め]し上[あ]がりたいのですが
why: 伺う humbly means 'to ask' a respected person; the other verbs have a different meaning or honour me.

jp: 来週[らいしゅう]の月曜日[げつようび]、先生[せんせい]のお宅[たく]に{伺[うかが]います/参[まい]ります|kg-ken-special}。
en: Next Monday I will visit my teacher's home.
why: Visiting a respected person's home is humble 伺う; いらっしゃる would honour me.

jp: 先生[せんせい]のご出身[しゅっしん]は北海道[ほっかいどう]だと{伺[うかが]いました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I heard that you are from Hokkaido, Teacher.
d: 拝見[はいけん]しました
why: I heard it from a respected person, which is expressed with the humble 伺う.

jp: 部長[ぶちょう]の昔[むかし]のお話[はなし]を、ぜひ{伺[うかが]いたいです|kg-ken-special}。
en: I would love to hear your stories from the old days, department head.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりたいです
why: Listening to a superior's story uses the humble 伺う; the others are about eating or saying.

jp: 駅[えき]への行[い]き方[かた]を先生[せんせい]に{伺[うかが]いました|kg-ken-special}。
en: I asked my teacher the way to the station.
d: 拝見[はいけん]しました
why: I asked a respected person for information, so the humble verb 伺う is used.

jp: お母様[かあさま]がご病気[びょうき]だと{伺[うかが]いました|kg-ken-special}が、いかがですか。
en: I heard that your mother is ill; how is she?
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: I heard news about the listener's mother, so humble 伺う is used for 'hear'.

jp: お忙[いそが]しいところ恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが、ご都合[つごう]を{伺[うかが]いたいのですが|kg-ken-special}。
en: I am sorry to trouble you when you are busy, but I would like to ask what time suits you.
d: おっしゃりたいのですが
召[め]し上[あ]がりたいのですが
申[もう]したいのですが
why: Asking a superior about their schedule is humble 伺う; the other verbs do not mean 'ask'.

jp: 先月[せんげつ]、取引先[とりひきさき]の工場[こうじょう]に{伺[うかが]いました/参[まい]りました|kg-ken-special}。
en: Last month I visited a client's factory.
d: 召[め]し上[あ]がりました
why: My own visit to a client's site is humble; いらっしゃる would raise me instead of the client.

jp: その件[けん]については、よく{存[ぞん]じております|kg-ken-special}。
en: I know that matter well.
why: I am the one who knows, so the humble 存じる is used; ご存じです refers to the listener's knowledge.

jp: 山田[やまだ]さんのことは、以前[いぜん]から{存[ぞん]じております|kg-ken-special}。
en: I have known of Mr. Yamada for some time.
d: 拝見[はいけん]しております
why: My own knowing is expressed with the humble 存じる, which is paired with ております.

jp: お名前[なまえ]は{存[ぞん]じております|kg-ken-special}が、お会[あ]いするのは初[はじ]めてです。
en: I know your name, but this is the first time we have met.
d: おっしゃっております
召[め]し上[あ]がっております
why: I know the other person's name, so humble 存じる is used; ご存じです would say that you know.

jp: 先生[せんせい]のご住所[じゅうしょ]は{存[ぞん]じません|kg-ken-special}。
en: I do not know your address, Teacher.
d: ご存[ぞん]じありません
why: The one who does not know is me, so the humble negative 存じません is used.

jp: 申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございませんが、そのお店[みせ]は{存[ぞん]じません|kg-ken-special}。
en: I am sorry, but I do not know that shop.
d: ご存[ぞん]じありません
召[め]し上[あ]がりません
why: The speaker's own lack of knowledge is 存じません; ご存じありません would say the listener does not know.

jp: 皆様[みなさま]、ご承知[しょうち]のことと{存[ぞん]じます|kg-ken-special}。
en: I trust that you are all aware of this.
why: 存じる also means 'to think, trust' in formal speech, with the speaker as the thinker.

jp: これは大変[たいへん]ありがたいことと{存[ぞん]じます|kg-ken-special}。
en: I consider this to be a great blessing.
why: I express my own thought politely, so 〜と存じます is used.

jp: その方[かた]のお電話番号[でんわばんごう]は{存[ぞん]じません|kg-ken-special}ので、お教[おし]えできません。
en: I do not know that person's phone number, so I cannot tell you.
d: ご存[ぞん]じありません
召[め]し上[あ]がりません
why: The speaker lacks the knowledge, so humble 存じません explains why they cannot answer.
